title: Northstar Insurance — Security Addendum Review (SIEM Audit Export + Logs)
summary: Northstar Procurement/Legal reviewed Redwood’s security addendum and focused on audit log export into their SIEM as a contractual control. Redwood confirmed the SIEM-ready audit export is in limited beta (hosted + dedicated), at-least-once delivery semantics, configurable filtering, and encryption/least-privilege controls. Northstar requested contract language for: (1) availability/notice around changes to audit events, (2) delivery guarantees and customer-side dedup expectations, (3) data residency and subprocessor coverage, (4) retention vs export responsibilities, and (5) timelines/commitment for GA. Redwood agreed to propose addendum language that positions SIEM export as a roadmap/beta feature for initial term unless they choose to condition go-live on GA; Redwood to provide a formal statement of controls and a beta limitations appendix. Next steps: Redwood legal to send redlines and a short “control description” paragraph for the addendum; Security to provide field-level PII stance (IP/user agent) and backfill limits in writing; follow-up call to finalize wording.
topics: Security addendum: audit logs + SIEM export as a required control
Beta scope and GA commitment language
Retention vs export responsibilities (SOC2/ISO questionnaire wording)
RBAC, least privilege, and evidence/auditability of export config changes
Encryption in transit/at rest; secrets handling; S3 KMS and cross-account role
questions: Can Northstar require SIEM export as a contractual obligation now, or must it be positioned as beta/roadmap until GA?
What are Redwood’s explicit delivery guarantees (SLOs) and what is excluded (downstream outage, customer misconfig)?
How long can Redwood backfill audit events after enabling export, and how is replay handled?
Will Redwood include source IP/user agent, and how is PII minimized/redacted?
Is there a change-management commitment for the audit schema (versioning, deprecation notice)?
next_steps: Redwood (Sofia) to send proposed addendum language: “Audit Events & Export” section + beta limitations appendix by 2025-04-25.
Redwood (Kevin/Naomi) to provide a written statement on delivery semantics (at-least-once), dedup guidance, and backfill window by 2025-04-25.
Northstar (Ravi/Janet) to review redlines internally and return comments by 2025-04-29.
Schedule 30-min follow-up to close legal wording and confirm go-live gating (beta vs GA) the week of 2025-04-29.
action_items: Sofia Mendes (Redwood) — Draft addendum redlines covering SIEM export, change management, and limitation of liability alignment — Due 2025-04-25
Kevin Osei (Redwood) — Send security control description: audit event contents, PII minimization, encryption, RBAC, retention vs export responsibilities — Due 2025-04-25
Naomi Feldman (Redwood) — Confirm current beta cohort posture + tentative GA window language acceptable for legal — Due 2025-04-25
Ravi Iyer (Northstar) — Provide Northstar required phrasing for “required security controls” and go-live criteria — Due 2025-04-29
Janet Morales (Northstar) — Confirm whether SIEM export must be contractual for signature or can be an exhibit/roadmap note — Due 2025-04-29
transcript:
Meeting: Northstar Insurance — Security Addendum Review (SIEM Audit Export + Logs)
Date/Time: Apr 23, 2025 2:00 PM ET
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees (Redwood): Liam O'Rourke; Sofia Mendes; Michael Grant; Kevin Osei; Naomi Feldman
Attendees (Northstar): Janet Morales; Ravi Iyer; Elena Petrova; Tom Erickson

—

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, I think we’re all here. Thanks everyone. This is Liam from Redwood. Goal today is to walk through the security addendum comments. I know SIEM export came up as like, a must-have control for you all. We’ve got Sofia from commercial counsel, Michael for privacy, Kevin from security engineering, and Naomi from product.

[00:19] Janet Morales: Great, thanks Liam. Yeah, we’re trying to get to signature, but we’ve got a few blockers. The big one is audit logs into Splunk.

[00:28] Ravi Iyer: And to be clear, the addendum currently says you “provide audit logs” but it doesn’t say export to customer SIEM. For us that’s not just nice-to-have, it’s a control requirement.

[00:41] Elena Petrova: Yep. We have a standard where critical vendors either integrate with our SIEM or provide a daily export to S3 that we ingest. Manual download from a console is not accepted.

[00:53] Liam O'Rourke: Makes sense. Maybe Kevin and Naomi, do you want to level set on where the SIEM-ready export is today?

[01:01] Naomi Feldman: Sure. So we’re building what we call SIEM-ready audit export. It’s in limited beta right now. Initial destinations are Splunk HEC, Datadog logs, and generic S3 delivery. Scope is hosted and dedicated deployments first. Private / on-prem is not in the beta scope.

[01:22] Naomi Feldman: The intent is you can configure filters, choose destinations, and we have delivery semantics that are at-least-once. Meaning you might see duplicates, but we provide stable event IDs and guidance on de-duping on your side.

[01:38] Ravi Iyer: Okay. So if it’s beta, can we still make it a contractual obligation?

[01:44] Sofia Mendes: We can talk about language options. Typically we avoid making beta functionality a hard obligation because it creates a mismatch with support and warranties. But we can commit to providing audit logs and we can include an exhibit describing the beta export capability and a target GA date as a roadmap commitment—depending on what your procurement requires.

[02:08] Janet Morales: Our template basically says “Vendor shall provide near real-time audit logs to Customer SIEM.” It’s… pretty standard for us.

[02:15] Sofia Mendes: Understood. Another approach is “Vendor will provide audit logs and supports export via SIEM integration as available,” with a mutually agreed implementation plan. Let’s keep going, I want to capture exactly what you need in the contract.

[02:33] Tom Erickson: One thing on my side: our vendor risk team needs a control statement. Like what events, retention, and who can access. If it’s only a product promise with no evidence, it’s hard.

[02:44] Kevin Osei: Yeah, we can provide a control description. On the event side: we have a canonical audit schema—event ID, timestamp, actor, action, resource, workspace/tenant, and where applicable source IP and user agent. We’re also doing PII minimization, so we don’t log full prompt payloads or customer content.

[03:05] Elena Petrova: You said “where applicable” for IP and user agent. We need that, like, for admin actions.

[03:12] Kevin Osei: For admin and auth-related events, yes. For some actions in the console and API we will include source IP and user agent when we have it. There are cases—like some system-to-system internal actions—where it may not be meaningful. But for user-initiated actions we’re aligning on capturing it.

[03:32] Michael Grant: And from privacy side, we’re careful that we’re not collecting more than we need. We treat IP as potentially sensitive; we include it as part of security logging, but we avoid anything like full request bodies. We can provide a field list in the appendix.

[03:47] Ravi Iyer: Good. For contractual language, we want (a) audit events are provided, (b) export is supported, (c) there is some stability. Like you can’t just remove fields without notice.

[03:58] Naomi Feldman: We can support versioning. Our schema has a v2 specifically to stabilize event_id and categories. If we make breaking changes, we’d deprecate with notice. We can propose a notice period.

[04:15] Sofia Mendes: Let’s talk specifics. Ravi, what notice period do you generally ask for? 30 days, 90 days?

[04:22] Ravi Iyer: For audit log schema changes, usually 90 days for breaking changes. Non-breaking changes okay.

[04:29] Sofia Mendes: Okay. That is reasonable. We’ll propose something like 90 days prior notice for material or breaking changes to audit event schema or export endpoints. With carve-outs for security emergencies.

[04:42] Janet Morales: Can you also commit to retention? Our questionnaire asks “how long are audit logs retained?”

[04:49] Kevin Osei: There are two concepts: Redwood retention internally vs export to your SIEM. Internally, we retain audit logs for a defined period (varies by plan), and export is a delivery mechanism so your SIEM becomes your system of record long-term.

[05:05] Michael Grant: In most SOC2 contexts, the language is “Vendor retains audit logs for X days” and “Customer is responsible for retention once exported.” We can provide that exact phrasing.

[05:16] Elena Petrova: What is X, though?

[05:18] Naomi Feldman: For enterprise, our standard is 180 days in-console for audit events. For beta, the exporter can backfill a limited window when you first enable it. We’re not doing unlimited historical export.

[05:34] Elena Petrova: How limited?

[05:36] Naomi Feldman: Current planned default is 7 days backfill, configurable up to a cap. We’re trying to avoid huge replays that spike volume and cost. For exceptions, we can coordinate via support.

[05:51] Ravi Iyer: If it’s 180 days retained, why can’t you export all 180 days?

[05:56] Kevin Osei: Technically possible, but it’s an operational risk in beta. The exporter is designed to be reliable, but backfilling months of data is basically a bulk export job. We can handle it with a managed engagement, but we don’t want to promise it as a self-serve feature in beta.

[06:15] Liam O'Rourke: And we want to be honest: this is precisely why we’re framing the exporter as beta for a small cohort. We can work with you on a plan that meets your audit requirements while we get to GA.

[06:30] Tom Erickson: Okay. I need to understand the delivery guarantee piece. “At-least-once” means duplicates, but does it also mean missing?

[06:40] Kevin Osei: The guarantee is we do not intentionally drop events; we retry with backoff and we checkpoint. If a destination is down or throttling, we may lag, but the system will keep trying. There’s also a dead-letter queue path for batches that repeatedly fail so operators can replay.

[06:59] Elena Petrova: In Splunk, we get throttled sometimes. How do you behave on 429s?

[07:05] Kevin Osei: We back off, and we batch. There are circuit breaker behaviors to avoid hammering. In extreme cases we can auto-pause export for that destination to protect the platform. But then we’d have to unpause once the downstream is healthy.

[07:24] Elena Petrova: Auto-pause makes me nervous if it means data gap.

[07:27] Kevin Osei: It’s not data loss. Events remain queued and lag increases. When unpaused, it continues. But yes, you would see a delay.

[07:39] Ravi Iyer: So contractually, can you say “near real-time”?

[07:43] Sofia Mendes: “Near real-time” is a loaded term. We can define an SLO like “most events delivered within X minutes under normal operating conditions.” But for beta, we typically avoid hard SLO commitments. What is your actual internal requirement?

[07:59] Elena Petrova: For critical actions, we prefer under 5 minutes. But for a vendor, 15 minutes is acceptable if we can demonstrate reliability.

[08:10] Naomi Feldman: Our internal target is in that range for normal conditions. We’re also instrumenting export lag metrics so you can see it.

[08:20] Tom Erickson: Can we have that in writing? Like not necessarily penalty, but at least a defined expectation.

[08:27] Sofia Mendes: Yes. We can include a statement of intended performance for beta and a GA SLA commitment once generally available. Or we can commit to providing you access to metrics and notify you of sustained lag beyond a threshold.

[08:46] Ravi Iyer: Another piece: we need to make sure your subprocessor list covers Splunk/Datadog. Actually we’re receiving the data, but you’re sending to our endpoint. Is Splunk a subprocessor in that model?

[08:58] Michael Grant: Good question. If you’re providing your own Splunk endpoint and token, Splunk is your processor on your side. Redwood is not engaging Splunk as a subprocessor in that path; we’re transmitting data to a customer-controlled destination. For Datadog, similarly, if you provide your API key and it goes to your account, that’s customer-directed processing.

[09:19] Ravi Iyer: We still want the contract to reflect that you’re initiating outbound transmissions to third parties.

[09:25] Michael Grant: Absolutely. We can address it under “Customer instructions / outbound integrations” and clarify responsibility boundaries.

[09:35] Janet Morales: And for S3, cross-account? We usually want vendors to write to a bucket in our account using a role. Not a vendor-owned bucket.

[09:46] Kevin Osei: Supported. The S3 destination supports assume-role for cross-account access and server-side encryption with KMS. We can provide the IAM policy snippet. Also we can require bucket encryption and reject destinations that are not encrypted.

[10:05] Elena Petrova: KMS key on our side, right? Customer-managed.

[10:08] Kevin Osei: Yes, customer-managed KMS is supported.

[10:13] Ravi Iyer: Okay. Back to the main. We have this clause: “Vendor shall provide audit logs to Customer SIEM for all administrative actions.” Can you do that?

[10:25] Naomi Feldman: We can provide export of audit events which include administrative actions, yes. But the caveat is it’s in beta. If your signature requires it to be warranted, we need to position it appropriately.

[10:41] Sofia Mendes: Here are two options:
1) We treat SIEM export as a condition of go-live rather than a warranty. So contract is signed, and deployment is contingent on successful SIEM export setup.
2) Or we attach it as an implementation exhibit with a stated timeline to GA and a right to terminate if not delivered by that date.

[11:05] Ravi Iyer: I like option two.

[11:07] Janet Morales: Procurement might be okay with that if we have dates.

[11:10] Liam O'Rourke: Naomi, what’s a responsible date to put?

[11:14] Naomi Feldman: For GA, I’m not going to promise a specific day, but we’re targeting late Q3 2025 for GA, assuming beta goes well. For your contract, we can propose language like “targeted” and with a review checkpoint.

[11:31] Ravi Iyer: Targeted is not binding. Our legal will ask for a drop-dead.

[11:36] Sofia Mendes: We can put a milestone-based commitment rather than a hard date: “Vendor will make commercially reasonable efforts to deliver GA in Q3 2025.” That’s common. Or a date with carve-outs.

[11:52] Elena Petrova: If it slips, we’re stuck.

[11:55] Liam O'Rourke: From customer success perspective, we can also structure it as: you join the beta cohort now (3–5 accounts), you get weekly check-ins, and if it fails to meet requirements, we pause rollout. But I hear you that legal wants teeth.

[12:12] Tom Erickson: We could accept “commercially reasonable” if we also have a right to terminate or not renew if the control isn’t met.

[12:21] Sofia Mendes: Okay. I’ll draft something that says: audit logs are provided; SIEM export is available in beta and will be made generally available under commercially reasonable efforts; if not available by X, customer may terminate the integration exhibit or delay go-live. We’ll propose language and you can redline.

[12:43] Ravi Iyer: Good. Another issue: liability and disclaimers. Our addendum forbids you from disclaiming security features.

[12:50] Sofia Mendes: Right. For beta features, we need to disclaim warranty. But we can keep the disclaimer limited to the exporter component and not general security obligations. Again, we’ll propose narrow language.

[13:06] Kevin Osei: One more technical detail that might matter to the clause: deduplication. Because it’s at-least-once, you should not treat “duplicate event” as an incident. The event_id will be stable, so Splunk can dedupe if you configure it.

[13:22] Elena Petrova: We can dedupe in Splunk, yes. But if you send the same event 100 times, that’s cost.

[13:29] Kevin Osei: Totally fair. We have controls to avoid replay storms. There’s a dead-letter queue and replay tooling with guardrails, and we cap retry rates.

[13:42] Tom Erickson: Can you put that into an assurance statement? Like “no more than…”

[13:48] Kevin Osei: I wouldn’t want to set a numeric bound in the contract. But we can describe the mechanism: retry with exponential backoff, checkpoints, operator review for repeated failures.

[14:03] Ravi Iyer: Okay. On access control: who can configure export? We need least privilege.

[14:10] Naomi Feldman: Admin-only. There are RBAC permissions specifically for creating/updating export configurations and rotating credentials. And changes to export config are themselves audited.

[14:23] Michael Grant: Also secrets handling: tokens and API keys are stored in our secrets manager; we don’t expose them in logs or UI. The UI uses references.

[14:34] Elena Petrova: And can we restrict which destination hosts you can send to? Like prevent someone from exfiltrating.

[14:42] Kevin Osei: We do destination validation and egress allowlisting at the platform layer. For Splunk/Datadog we validate known host patterns. For S3, it’s AWS. If you need custom endpoints, we review.

[14:58] Ravi Iyer: Great. That helps with internal approval.

[15:02] Janet Morales: So, what do we need from you after this call?

[15:06] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll send (1) proposed redlines / language for the addendum, (2) a short one-pager describing the SIEM export capability and limitations, and (3) the security control description for audit logs—fields, retention, access control.

[15:22] Naomi Feldman: And I can also confirm whether we can include Northstar in the beta cohort. It depends on region and deployment model.

[15:29] Elena Petrova: We’re hosted in US-East initially, maybe dedicated later. No on-prem.

[15:35] Naomi Feldman: That’s within the supported beta scope.

[15:41] Ravi Iyer: Another contractual thing: data residency. If you export from US-East, does anything cross regions?

[15:48] Kevin Osei: The exporter runs in-region with the tenant. For hosted and dedicated, we keep processing in the selected region. The outbound destination is up to you—your Splunk endpoint or S3 bucket region. We can document it.

[16:06] Michael Grant: And we can include an explicit statement: audit events are generated and processed within the tenant’s region, subject to limited support access exceptions, etc.

[16:18] Tom Erickson: Perfect.

[16:21] (brief crosstalk)

[16:24] Janet Morales: I want to be mindful of time. Can we go line-by-line on the addendum clause we flagged?

[16:30] Sofia Mendes: Yes. I have your redline open. Clause 4.2 “Audit Logging.” It currently says “Vendor will maintain audit logs of administrative actions and provide access via the service.” Your proposed change adds “and export to Customer SIEM within 5 minutes.”

[16:51] Ravi Iyer: Correct.

[16:53] Sofia Mendes: We can accept “maintain audit logs of administrative actions.” We can also accept “provide export” but not “within 5 minutes” as a hard SLA in the addendum today, especially for beta.

[17:06] Elena Petrova: Could we say “promptly”?

[17:09] Sofia Mendes: We can define “promptly” as “typically within 15 minutes under normal operating conditions.” But we would need carve-outs. Another way: we can provide an SLO in an exhibit that’s not a breach unless it’s sustained.

[17:28] Ravi Iyer: Okay. Put it in an exhibit.

[17:31] Sofia Mendes: Great. Next, your clause adds “logs shall include source IP, user agent, and immutable identifiers.” Kevin, can you support that?

[17:41] Kevin Osei: Immutable identifier: yes, event_id. Source IP and user agent: for user-initiated admin actions, yes. There may be cases where user agent is not available. We can say “where available.”

[17:56] Ravi Iyer: “Where available” is fine if you also commit to collecting it.

[18:01] Kevin Osei: We can say “Vendor will make commercially reasonable efforts to capture source IP and user agent for user-initiated actions.”

[18:12] Michael Grant: And I’d add: subject to applicable law and data minimization principles.

[18:19] Ravi Iyer: Okay.

[18:21] Sofia Mendes: Next, “Customer may retain logs for 7 years.” That’s on your side. We’ll clarify that retention after export is Customer-controlled.

[18:31] Janet Morales: Right.

[18:33] Sofia Mendes: Next, the clause asks for “no less than 365 days retention” by Redwood. Naomi said 180 days.

[18:41] Naomi Feldman: Correct, 180 days is our standard enterprise retention in the console today.

[18:46] Ravi Iyer: That’s not enough for some of our audits.

[18:49] Michael Grant: Usually that’s why SIEM export exists. Vendors don’t want to be long-term record keepers for 7 years; the customer SIEM is.

[18:59] Elena Petrova: If export is reliable, 180 days is okay. But if export is beta, we need a bridge.

[19:08] Naomi Feldman: Understood. For the bridge, we can do two things: ensure you’re in beta and have a support plan; and if needed, provide a managed backfill or periodic bulk export to S3 while beta stabilizes.

[19:24] Ravi Iyer: Managed backfill would help. Can it be in the contract?

[19:28] Sofia Mendes: We can include it as an optional professional services / support item, not as an unconditional obligation. We can state that Redwood will provide reasonable assistance with initial export enablement and backfill as part of onboarding for enterprise.

[19:44] Janet Morales: That sounds workable.

[19:47] Tom Erickson: We also need auditability of who changed settings. If someone changes export filter to exclude events, that’s a problem.

[19:55] Naomi Feldman: Config changes are audited as events. Filters also default to include security-relevant categories. You can choose to filter down, but that action is logged and requires admin permissions.

[20:11] Elena Petrova: Is there a way to lock it? Like, prevent changes.

[20:15] Naomi Feldman: Not in beta. In GA, we might add change approvals. But today the control is RBAC + audit trail.

[20:25] Ravi Iyer: Okay.

[20:27] Sofia Mendes: Let’s capture as: “Changes to audit export configuration are logged and available for review,” and optionally “Customer can restrict configuration access via RBAC.”

[20:39] (pause)

[20:41] Liam O'Rourke: I’m going to note that as an item in the exhibit.

[20:45] Elena Petrova: One more: if your exporter is down, do we get notified?

[20:50] Kevin Osei: We have operational visibility—metrics, dashboards, and alerts. In beta, we can set up proactive notifications if lag crosses a threshold. For GA, we can integrate with our incident comms.

[21:05] Tom Erickson: We want that in writing too.

[21:09] Sofia Mendes: We can include a service notification clause: security incidents and material service outages. For exporter-specific issues, we can commit to notifying you of sustained failures during beta check-ins.

[21:22] Ravi Iyer: We prefer an email notification within 24 hours of discovering sustained failure.

[21:29] Sofia Mendes: That’s reasonable. We’ll propose.

[21:34] Janet Morales: Okay, we’re getting somewhere.

[21:37] Liam O'Rourke: Quick check: anything else blocking signature besides SIEM export language?

[21:42] Janet Morales: Mostly that. And the limitation that it’s beta—we need to reconcile that.

[21:48] Ravi Iyer: Also the phrase “as-is” in the beta section. Remove that or narrow it.

[21:55] Sofia Mendes: We’ll narrow it.

[21:58] Michael Grant: And I’ll provide a short privacy note that audit logs exclude customer content, which often helps your DPA review.

[22:07] Elena Petrova: That’s helpful. Our team asked if prompts are logged. So answer is no.

[22:12] Kevin Osei: Correct. We avoid prompts and model outputs in audit events.

[22:17] (crosstalk)

[22:20] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, we can shift to wrap-up unless there’s anything else.

[22:24] Ravi Iyer: One last: if you change the audit schema, we need notice. We said 90 days.

[22:30] Sofia Mendes: Got it. We’ll propose 90 days for material/breaking changes, plus an emergency carve-out.

[22:37] Tom Erickson: And can you provide sample events? Like what Splunk sees.

[22:41] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we can provide sample payloads. Not a full deck, but a few example events and mapping.

[22:50] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[22:52] Liam O'Rourke: I’ll recap next steps:
- Sofia will send proposed addendum language and an exhibit for the SIEM export beta + intended GA.
- Kevin and Naomi will send a control description: what we log, delivery semantics, backfill limits, and dedup guidance.
- Northstar will review and return redlines by end of next week.
- We’ll schedule a follow-up to close.

[23:14] Janet Morales: Works.

[23:16] Ravi Iyer: Works.

[23:18] Elena Petrova: Works.

[23:20] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Thanks everyone.

[23:23] (Call continues with light scheduling / off-topic chatter; transcript truncated by Fireflies summarization)

[23:30] Janet Morales: Liam, just send me the redlines to my email and I’ll route.

[23:34] Liam O'Rourke: Will do.

[23:36] Sofia Mendes: Thanks all.

[23:38] (end)

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies):
- Customer requires SIEM export of audit logs as contractual security control.
- Redwood: SIEM-ready audit export is limited beta; hosted + dedicated; Splunk/Datadog/S3.
- Proposed approach: exhibit + commercially reasonable GA commitment; define expectations for lag + notice for breaking schema changes.
- Customer requests: 90-day notice for schema changes, clarify IP/user agent availability, clarify retention vs export responsibilities.
